# Stormdrive The Class IV storm drive is the fusion reactor fitted to most ships. It injects plasma into a fission core and turns the heat into electricity. It is a simple machine to connect: fuel goes in one pipe, nucleium waste comes out the other.
## Getting one The drive is sold by cargo as a flatpack, or printed from the engineering tech tree once researched. Use a multitool on the flatpack and wait for it to unfold. It needs bare plating under its 3x1 body: pull up finished floor and clear primary-layer pipes, atmos devices, crates and tanks across all three tiles first; cables and off-layer pipes are fine. Unlike the RBMK it brings no footing or cabling: it drops the drive alone, so run the fuel and waste lines and the HV cable yourself. A cold, shut-down drive built from a flatpack can be packed back into its flatpack from the context menu; a running or melting drive cannot. The flatpack does not include control rods. They are printed separately, and the drive is not safe to light without them.
## Before you start - Mount five control rods in the rod bay. The drive cannot cool without them. - Fill the fuel line with [bold]plasma[/bold]. Tritium is the high-yield alternative once you know the machine, but it runs hotter and cools worse. - Set the control rods to AZ-5 (100 %) before fuelling. A cold core is a safe core. - Ignite with the particle accelerator. A level-3 shot carries enough heat on its own.
## The console The console is linked to the drive with a multitool. It shows:
- [bold]Core temperature[/bold] — colour-coded against the hot, critical and meltdown thresholds. - [bold]Stability[/bold] — the 0–100 safety margin, with a line underneath naming what is moving it. The small [bold]?[/bold] next to the bar repeats this page in short form. - [bold]Control rods[/bold] — the mean integrity of the mounted rods. - [bold]Output[/bold] — the power actually delivered last cycle. - [bold]Reaction rate[/bold] — how fast the core is eating its fuel, in moles per second. - [bold]Fuel ratio[/bold] — the share of the fuel line that is plasma or tritium. - [bold]Fuel moles[/bold] — the total gas in the line, against the over-pressure bands. - [bold]Fuel line composition[/bold] — every gas, with a rolling graph.
## Stability Stability is the drive's safety margin. The control rods do not touch it; only the fuel line does. It recovers while the mix is rich and the line is not over-pressurised, and it bleeds away when the mix is lean, the line is over pressure, or the core is starved of fuel. The stability bar on the console, and the line of text under it, tell you which of those is happening right now.
The drive works in two-second cycles, and stability moves once per cycle:
- [bold]Fuel ratio 25 % or more, fuel moles under the amber line:[/bold] +0.5 per cycle, recovering. - [bold]Rich but over the amber line:[/bold] the recovery is cancelled; −0.01 per cycle. - [bold]Fuel ratio 12.5–25 %:[/bold] −0.01 per cycle. - [bold]Lean and over the line:[/bold] −0.52 per cycle. - [bold]Fuel below 12.5 %, or fewer moles than one cycle of throughput:[/bold] −1 per cycle. The reaction stops, heat falls, and stability dies. A falling temperature is not proof of safety.
Below 75, every cycle has a chance of a jolt: half the time the core takes a burst of heat, the other half the reaction rate itself jumps by a fifth to a third. That heat burst is checked against the meltdown threshold in the same cycle, so a hot core with low stability can arm a meltdown without the temperature ever looking alarming. Below 15, the core starts tearing anomalies loose.
[bold]The two fuel bars are the controls.[/bold] Keep both green. The Fuel Moles bar turns amber above [bold]24 × the reaction rate in mol/s + 20[/bold] moles; the Fuel Ratio bar turns green at 25 % fuel. If either is not green, recovery has stopped or is about to, so treat it as a warning light rather than a promise. The mole threshold moves with the reaction rate, so a reaction that slows down can turn a previously safe mole count into over pressure.
## Presets - [bold]AZ-1 (0 %):[/bold] rods fully withdrawn. Maximum reactivity and cooling disabled. This is the meltdown setting. - [bold]AZ-2 (5 %):[/bold] hot operation, about 720 °C. Only for a core with high stability and a raised meltdown threshold. - [bold]AZ-3 (16 %):[/bold] nominal, about 340 °C. - [bold]AZ-4 (33.6 %):[/bold] cold start, about 100 °C. - [bold]AZ-5 (100 %):[/bold] SCRAM. Rods fully inserted; the core cools to zero. - [bold]AZ-6:[/bold] maintenance. Only from idle. - [bold]AZ-7:[/bold] fuel dump. Moves the fuel line to the waste line.
Rod wear scales with output and insertion depth, so a long SCRAM wears rods faster than a relaxed 33.6 % setting. Check the rod integrity bar. At 0 % integrity the rods fail and cooling stops entirely, which is a different failure path from low stability.
## Gases - [bold]Plasma:[/bold] the standard fuel. It feeds the reaction, but it lowers power per mole. - [bold]Tritium:[/bold] high-yield fuel. It feeds the reaction much harder, raises power and raises the meltdown threshold, but lowers cooling. Treat it as a hot-rodding option, not a default. - [bold]Oxygen:[/bold] power. Raises the power multiplier; no effect on stability. - [bold]Nitrogen:[/bold] moderator. Lowers the reaction rate and raises cooling; useful for keeping a hot core controllable. - [bold]Carbon dioxide:[/bold] moderator. Raises cooling and lowers power. - [bold]Water vapour:[/bold] lowers the reaction rate. A shutdown gas. - [bold]Nitrous oxide:[/bold] raises the temperature thresholds, including meltdown, at the cost of faster rod wear. - [bold]Nucleium:[/bold] waste. It lowers cooling and the meltdown threshold and reduces power. Vent the waste line; do not let it back up into the fuel line.
Plasma and nitrogen cancel each other's reaction-rate contribution at a 1:1 ratio. A mix of 33 % plasma, 33 % oxygen and 33 % nitrogen therefore has a net reaction-rate modifier of zero, and the reaction barely runs at low temperature. Use more plasma or less nitrogen if you want power.
## Meltdown The core melts down when its temperature passes the meltdown threshold. On a plain plasma mix that is 800 °C; nitrous oxide and tritium raise it, nucleium lowers it. The drive gives you an 18-second fuse, but it also destroys every control rod when the fuse starts, so cooling is off for the whole countdown. The only way to survive an armed fuse is to starve the reaction (fuel below 12.5 %), which makes the core lose 5 °C per cycle; if you were barely over the line, that can save you.
If the core is hot and stability is low, do not wait for the alarm:
- [bold]SCRAM[/bold] to 100 % and keep the fuel ratio rich. The rods reduce the reaction rate, which shrinks the stability heat bursts. - [bold]Lower the input pressure[/bold] if the Fuel Moles bar is amber or red. - [bold]Add moderator[/bold] (nitrogen or carbon dioxide) if the core is above 670 °C; at that point even a full SCRAM cannot out-cool the heat term without it. - [bold]If it is already armed,[/bold] dump the fuel or flood the line with nitrogen or carbon dioxide to starve the reaction, and hope you were only just over the threshold.
A full shutdown below 20 °C resets stability to 100 on the next ignition. That is the clean way out of a low-stability spiral.
## Repairing a meltdown A melted drive is a wreck, not scrap. It keeps irradiating until it is repaired, but it can be brought back to a factory-fresh state in four steps. Each step takes five seconds, requires you to stay adjacent, and is cancelled if you move or take damage.
- [bold]Clear the pit.[/bold] Shovel the plutonium sludge out. The sludge is dumped on the floor, so suit up for radiation and clean it away before it spreads. - [bold]Reline the pit.[/bold] Use [bold]25 sheets of uranium[/bold] on the drive. Other sheet metals do not count. - [bold]Weld the liner.[/bold] Use a welder on the drive. - [bold]Install a new core.[/bold] Use a [bold]Class IV nuclear storm drive reactor core[/bold]. It is a two-handed item: both hands must be free to carry it and to install it. The installation destroys every control rod left in the bay and resets the drive to cold idle, so there is no point pulling the old rods first.
The core is printed from the [bold]Fission Basics[/bold] research node. Once it is in, mount five fresh control rods and refuel the line before you light the drive again; the repair resets the reaction, not the piping.
